items.prose: Three episodes of a fixed policy, $\gamma = 1$. State P is first visited with these rewards still to come: (2, 3), (−1, 2), (0, 0, 3). Episode 3 visits P a second time, before its final reward.
items.question: What is the first-visit Monte Carlo estimate of $v(P)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum each episode's rewards after P, then average.

byKey.first-r: You averaged the first rewards only: 2, −1 and 0.
byKey.first-only: That is episode 1 alone. Average all three first-visit returns.
byKey.sum: That is the total. Divide by three.

explain.text: First-visit returns are $2 + 3 = 5$, $-1 + 2 = 1$ and $0 + 0 + 3 = 3$, averaging 3. The second visit in episode 3 does not count for first-visit MC.

items.prose: $V(s) = 1.0$ and $V(s') = 2.0$. A step from $s$ to $s'$ pays 0.4. $\alpha = 0.2$, $\gamma = 0.9$.
items.question: What is the new $V(s)$ after TD(0)? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute $\delta$, then add a fifth of it.

byKey.delta: That is $\delta$. Add $0.2\delta$ to the old value.
byKey.full: You moved all the way to the target.

items.prose: Q-learning on the deterministic grid: $Q(\text{r3c4}, U) = 0.3$. Moving U reaches row 2, column 4, where the four $Q$ values are 0.50, 0.20, 0.10 and 0.40. $\alpha = 0.1$, $\gamma = 0.9$.
items.question: What is the new $Q(\text{r3c4}, U)$? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the largest next value, 0.50.

byKey.avg: You averaged the next values; Q-learning takes the max.
byKey.target: That is the target; move a tenth of the way.
byKey.no-step: You left out the step cost.

explain.text: Q-learning's target takes the best next value, 0.50: $-0.04 + 0.45 = 0.41$. The update adds a tenth of $0.41 - 0.3$, giving 0.311.

items.prose: At a cliff edge, reward −1; the agent's next action (a random one) has $Q = -60$, while the best next action has $Q = -8$. $\gamma = 1$, $Q(s, a) = -10$, $\alpha = 0.5$.
items.question: What is SARSA's new $Q(s, a)$? Give a decimal to 1 place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. SARSA uses the action actually taken next.

byKey.target: That is the target; move half way.

explain.text: SARSA's target $-1 - 60 = -61$ gives $-10 + 0.5 \times (-51) = -35.5$; it reflects the random move it is about to make; Q-learning's, $-9$, ignores it. That is why SARSA learns to avoid edges while exploring.

items.prose: An episode pays 2, 0, −1, 4 on its four steps. $\gamma = 0.5$.
items.question: What is $G_0$? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work back with $G_t = R_{t+1} + 0.5 G_{t+1}$.

byKey.disc-first: You discounted the first reward too.

items.prose: A state's Monte Carlo returns have standard deviation 0.5.
items.question: How many first visits give a standard error of 0.02?

byKey.var: You used the variance 0.25 as if it were the standard deviation.

explain.text: $n = (0.5/0.02)^2 = 625$. Quartering the error would take 16 times as many.

items.prose: Two agents learn on the same hazardous task, both exploring with $\varepsilon = 0.1$ for ever.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: SARSA values its exploring policy; Q-learning the greedy one
Both learn the same values, so they pick the same route
options.why: They agree only when exploring stops. With $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the targets differ.

options.text: Q-learning learns the safer route, since it takes the max
options.why: The max ignores its own random moves, so it keeps the risky route.
Both learn; they learn different things.

explain.text: SARSA's target uses the action actually taken, exploring and all; Q-learning's uses the max. With exploring that never stops, they settle on different routes.

items.prose: A learned greedy policy differs from value iteration's arg-max in two cells of the deterministic grid. In both cells, U and R lead to cells of equal value.
items.question: Is the learned policy optimal?

options.text: Yes: in those cells both moves are in the optimal set
No: it disagrees with value iteration
options.why: Value iteration's arg-max picked one of two equal moves; the other is as good.

options.text: Only if Q equals V to 4 places
options.why: The policy can be optimal before the values settle.
It may never agree exactly in a tie, and need not.

feedback.correct: Check membership in the optimal set.

explain.text: Compare policies by optimal sets. Equal moves are equally optimal.

items.prose: A constant step size $\alpha$ averages roughly the last $1/\alpha$ targets.
items.question: Which $\alpha$ leaves the noisiest estimates once learning has settled?

options.why: 0.02 averages about 50 targets: the least noisy, but the slowest.

options.text: They are all the same once settled
options.why: The step size sets how much noise remains.

feedback.correct: Half a step per target keeps only about 2 targets' worth of averaging.

explain.text: With $\alpha = 0.5$ each estimate is mostly the last two targets. Smaller steps average more and settle tighter, but learn more slowly.

items.prose: A market-making simulation runs without ever ending.
items.question: Which method can evaluate its policy?

options.why: Monte Carlo needs a return, which needs an end.
Only TD can update without an end.

feedback.correct: TD needs one step at a time.
feedback.generic: Which method waits for the end?

explain.text: TD(0) updates after each step, so it works without episodes; the discount keeps values finite.
